name: Spoon busk

card.summary: A curved, rigid front panel for a corset that keeps the torso upright and gives the abdomen a smooth, rounded line under clothes.
card.note: Historical corsetry part from the 1870s; modern corsetry makers still use busks.

quick.overview:
A spoon busk is a stiff steel or similar front stay in a corset, curved outward at the lower end like the bowl of a spoon. It was developed in the second half of the nineteenth century. It gives a smooth, upright front line and shapes the stomach into a rounder profile.

The appearance payoff is a defined, upright torso silhouette while the corset is worn. Descriptions come from corsetry history; no clinical trials have examined it as a posture aid.
quick.how: It sits in the centre front of a corset, either as a flat panel in a pocket or as a two-part busk that fastens like hooks and posts. The curved lower end lies over the lower abdomen to spread pressure and stop the corset's hard lower edge from jutting out. It is worn as part of a full corset.
quick.risks: Tight corsetry in general can restrict breathing and movement and cause discomfort, and there is no clinical data on the spoon busk specifically. Modern corset braces for back support are sold for mild to moderate back pain and are sometimes prescribed after spinal surgery.

lead: A spoon busk is a rigid, curved element placed at the centre front of a corset. The general busk is a stiff, flat piece along the sternum that keeps the torso upright and creates a smooth front line, and the spoon busk adds a broadened, outward-curving lower end shaped like a spoon.[1][2]

It was invented in the second half of the nineteenth century, around the 1870s, and was intended to shape the stomach into a rounder look, to keep the corset's rigid lower edge from jutting out and to spread pressure across the abdomen.[1][2] For people interested in appearance it matters as a historical tool for sculpting posture and silhouette.

angle.text: Corsetry histories describe the busk as the part that keeps the front straight and upright. The spoon busk rounds out the abdomen and spreads pressure, giving a smoother front under clothing.

paras: Busks are of two types. Single-piece busks, made of wood, ivory, bone or baleen, were slipped into a pocket in the garment and tied with a lace called the busk point; baleen busks appear in the wardrobe accounts of Elizabeth I in the 1580s.[1] A new two-part form of steel appeared in the mid-nineteenth century, with one piece carrying loops and the other posts that work like hook-and-eye fastenings, which made corsets much easier to put on and take off.[1]

The spoon busk was developed later, in the 1870s, and is described as shaping the stomach into a rounder look, spreading pressure across the abdomen and keeping the corset's lower edge from jutting out.[2]

Early stays were valued for providing posture and smooth body contours, and corsets were linked to an upright, military-style bearing.[2] Single-piece busks were meant to keep the front straight, supporting an upright posture, and were often carved or inscribed and given as courtship gifts.[1] Victorian centre-front split busks let wearers fasten the corset in front without help.[2]

Corset braces resemble traditional corsets but use elastic fabric and plastic boning, and they support the lower back for mild to moderate back pain and are sometimes prescribed after spinal surgery.[2] Neck corsets, a type of posture collar, are not considered true corsets, and the article says they do not produce lasting posture results.[2]

timeline.event: Baleen busks appear in Elizabeth I's wardrobe accounts.[1]
